units.title: Foundations of Government
units.blurb: Why governments exist, the forms they take, the ideas of natural rights and the social contract, models of democracy, and the rule of law. AP Unit 1.

units.title: The Founding Documents
units.blurb: English roots, the Declaration of Independence, the Articles of Confederation, the Convention and its compromises, The Federalist and the Anti-Federalists, and the Bill of Rights. AP Unit 1.

units.title: The Constitution, Article by Article
units.blurb: The Preamble and the seven articles, separation of powers, checks and balances, and how the Constitution is amended. AP Unit 1.

units.title: Federalism
units.blurb: How power is divided between the nation and the states: enumerated, reserved and concurrent powers, the Supremacy and Necessary and Proper Clauses, the commerce power, money and mandates, and relations among the states. AP Unit 1.

units.title: Congress
units.blurb: The House and the Senate, apportionment and districts, the powers of Congress, its leaders and committees, how a bill becomes law, the filibuster, the budget and oversight, and how members represent. AP Unit 2.

units.title: The Presidency and the Executive Branch
units.blurb: Who may be President and who succeeds, formal and informal powers, the bureaucracy, impeachment and war powers. AP Unit 2.

units.title: The Courts
units.blurb: The federal court system, how the Supreme Court decides, judicial review, how judges are chosen, ways of reading the Constitution, and checks on the courts. AP Unit 2.

units.title: Civil Liberties
units.blurb: The Bill of Rights, incorporation, the freedoms of religion, speech and the press, the right to bear arms, the rights of the accused and privacy. AP Unit 3.

units.title: Civil Rights
units.blurb: Equal protection, the major civil rights laws, the amendments that widened the vote, and how courts protect minorities in a system of majority rule. AP Unit 3.

units.title: Citizenship and Participation
units.blurb: How people become citizens, citizens' rights and duties, voting and turnout, how political views form, public opinion, interest groups and the media. AP Units 4 and 5.

units.title: Elections and Parties
units.blurb: Political parties and the two-party system, primaries and conventions, the Electoral College, money in campaigns and congressional elections. AP Unit 5.

units.title: State, Local and Tribal Government
units.blurb: State governments and constitutions, counties, cities and school districts, direct democracy, and tribal nations.

units.title: Citizenship Test Practice
units.blurb: Mixed practice on the history and government questions of the U.S. naturalization civics test, built on the units of this course.

topics.title: Why We Have Government
topics.short: Governments keep order, provide security and public goods, protect rights and settle disputes; the Preamble lists six purposes, from "a more perfect Union" to "the Blessings of Liberty."
topics.trouble: Students confuse the purposes of government with its powers. A purpose is a goal ("insure domestic Tranquility"); a power is a means (to tax, to raise an army).

topics.title: Forms of Government
topics.short: Governments differ by who rules: one person (monarchy, dictatorship), a few (oligarchy) or the people (democracy, direct or representative); a republic is governed by elected representatives, and authoritarian and totalitarian states allow no real opposition.
topics.trouble: Students think "democracy" and "republic" are opposites. The United States is a representative democracy and a republic: people rule through elected representatives, under a constitution.

topics.title: Natural Rights and the Social Contract
topics.short: Hobbes argued people accept government to escape a "war of all against all"; Locke held that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property and may replace a government that violates them; Montesquieu urged separating powers.
topics.trouble: Students credit Locke with "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness." Locke wrote of life, liberty and property (estate); "the pursuit of Happiness" is Jefferson's phrase in the Declaration.

topics.title: Models of Democracy
topics.short: Political scientists describe participatory democracy (broad participation by citizens), pluralist democracy (groups compete for influence) and elite democracy (a few well-informed leaders and groups decide); each can be seen in American institutions.
topics.trouble: Students treat the models as rival governments to pick from. They are lenses for describing the same system: a town meeting looks participatory, interest-group bargaining pluralist, the Electoral College and Senate partly elite.

topics.title: Limited Government and the Rule of Law
topics.short: Under the rule of law, laws are public, apply equally to everyone, including officials, and are enforced by fair procedures; limited government means a constitution sets what officials may and may not do.
topics.trouble: Students think the rule of law means following whatever the government says. It means the government itself is bound by law, and no one is above it.

topics.title: English and Colonial Roots
topics.short: American government drew on Magna Carta (1215), the English Bill of Rights (1689), the Mayflower Compact (1620), colonial charters and assemblies, and the idea that the people's representatives must consent to taxes.
topics.trouble: Students think Magna Carta guaranteed rights to everyone. In 1215 it protected mainly the barons' rights against the king; its later meaning, that the ruler is under the law, grew over centuries.

topics.title: The Ideas of the Declaration
topics.short: The Declaration of Independence (1776) states that people have unalienable rights, that governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed," and that the people may alter or abolish a government that destroys those ends; its grievances accuse the King.
topics.trouble: Students think the Declaration is law that courts enforce. It is a founding statement of principles; the Constitution is the supreme law.

topics.title: The Articles of Confederation
topics.short: The Articles (1781 to 1789) left power with the states: Congress could not tax, regulate trade between states or enforce laws; there was no executive or national court; laws needed nine states and amendments all thirteen.
topics.trouble: Students think the Articles created no national government. There was a Congress with real powers (war, treaties, western lands); it lacked the power to tax and enforce.

topics.title: The Convention and Its Compromises
topics.short: The 1787 Convention settled conflicts by compromise: the Great Compromise (a House by population, a Senate with two per state), the Three-Fifths Compromise, the slave trade clause (no ban before 1808) and the Electoral College.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the Virginia and New Jersey Plans. Virginia (large states): representation by population; New Jersey (small states): one state, one vote.

topics.title: The Federalist and the Anti-Federalists
topics.short: In Federalist No. 10 Madison argued a large republic controls factions; in No. 51 that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition"; Brutus No. 1 warned that a large republic would be too distant from the people and that the national government's powers would swallow the states.
topics.trouble: Students think Federalist No. 10 wants to abolish factions. Madison says removing the causes of faction would destroy liberty, so the remedy is to control their effects through a large republic.

topics.title: Ratification and the Bill of Rights
topics.short: The Constitution took effect when nine states ratified (1788); several states ratified only with calls for amendments, and the First Congress proposed the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791.
topics.trouble: Students think all states ratified right away. North Carolina (1789) and Rhode Island (1790) ratified after the new government had already begun.

topics.title: The Preamble
topics.short: The Preamble begins "We the People" and lists six goals: union, justice, domestic tranquility, the common defense, the general welfare and the blessings of liberty.
topics.trouble: Students think the Preamble grants powers. It states purposes; courts have not treated it as a source of power.

topics.title: Article I: The Legislative Branch
topics.short: Article I creates Congress, sets the House and Senate's makeup, lists its powers in Section 8 (taxing, borrowing, commerce, coining money, declaring war and more, ending with the Necessary and Proper Clause), and limits Congress and the states in Sections 9 and 10.
topics.trouble: Students think Article I lists everything Congress may do in detail. Section 8 lists the enumerated powers, and the Necessary and Proper Clause adds the means to carry them out.

topics.title: Article II: The Executive Branch
topics.short: Article II vests "the executive Power" in a President, sets qualifications and the Electoral College, and names powers: commander in chief, treaties (with two-thirds of the Senate), appointments (with Senate consent), pardons and the duty to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed."
topics.trouble: Students think the President can make treaties alone. Treaties need the consent of two-thirds of the senators present.

topics.title: Article III: The Judicial Branch
topics.short: Article III creates the Supreme Court, lets Congress create lower courts, gives judges tenure "during good Behaviour" and pay that cannot be cut, lists the kinds of cases federal courts hear, guarantees jury trials for crimes and defines treason.
topics.trouble: Students think Article III sets the number of justices at nine. The number is set by Congress; it has been nine since 1869.

topics.title: Articles IV to VII
topics.short: Article IV: full faith and credit, privileges and immunities, new states and a republican form of government; Article V: amendments; Article VI: the Supremacy Clause, oaths and no religious test for office; Article VII: ratification by nine states.
topics.trouble: Students put the Supremacy Clause in Article I. It is in Article VI: the Constitution, federal laws made under it and treaties are "the supreme Law of the Land."

topics.title: Separation of Powers
topics.short: The Constitution gives lawmaking to Congress, carrying out the laws to the President and deciding cases to the courts, so no one branch holds all power.
topics.trouble: Students think separation means the branches never share a task. The branches are separate institutions that share powers, such as lawmaking (the veto) and appointments (Senate consent).

topics.title: Checks and Balances
topics.short: Each branch can check the others: the veto and the override, Senate confirmation of judges, judicial review, impeachment, Congress's control of money, and the President's power to nominate judges.
topics.trouble: Students mix up which branch checks which. Name the check, then its actor and its target: the veto is the President checking Congress; an override is Congress checking the President.

topics.title: Amending the Constitution
topics.short: Amendments are proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention called by two-thirds of the states, never yet used) and ratified by three-fourths of the states (38 of 50), through legislatures or conventions; there are 27 amendments.
topics.trouble: Students think the President signs amendments or that a national vote ratifies them. The President has no formal role, and ratification is by the states.

topics.title: Dividing Power: Federal, State and Shared
topics.short: Federalism divides power: the national government has enumerated (delegated) powers such as coining money and war; the Tenth Amendment reserves other powers to the states or the people; both share concurrent powers such as taxing and making courts.
topics.trouble: Students mix up federalism with separation of powers. Federalism divides power between levels (nation and states); separation of powers divides it among branches at one level.

topics.title: Supremacy and Necessary and Proper
topics.short: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Court held that the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose reasonable means, such as a national bank, and that under the Supremacy Clause a state may not tax a federal bank.
topics.trouble: Students think "necessary" means absolutely necessary. Marshall read it as "convenient" or "useful": appropriate means plainly adapted to a legitimate end.

topics.title: The Commerce Power
topics.short: Congress may regulate commerce "among the several States"; the Court read the power broadly for decades (Gibbons v. Ogden, 1824; the New Deal cases) and then set limits in United States v. Lopez (1995), which struck down a federal ban on guns near schools.
topics.trouble: Students think the Commerce Clause covers only goods crossing a state line. Since the 1940s it has covered activities that substantially affect interstate commerce, with limits since Lopez.

topics.title: Grants and Mandates
topics.short: Washington shapes state policy with money: categorical grants (for specific purposes, with conditions), block grants (broad purposes, more state choice) and mandates (federal requirements, some unfunded); conditions on grants are a main tool, within limits the Court has set.
topics.trouble: Students mix up categorical and block grants. Categorical grants come with narrow purposes and strings; block grants give states wider discretion.

topics.title: Relations Among the States
topics.short: Article IV requires states to give full faith and credit to each other's public acts and court judgments, to give citizens of other states the same basic privileges and immunities, and to return people charged with crimes (extradition); states may also make compacts with Congress's consent.
topics.trouble: Students think a state must treat out-of-state people the same in every respect. Privileges and immunities covers fundamental matters such as earning a living; states may still charge nonresidents more for things like hunting licenses or public college tuition.

topics.title: The House and the Senate
topics.short: The House has 435 members, elected every two years, at least 25 years old and seven years a citizen; the Senate has 100 members, two per state, six-year terms with a third elected every two years, at least 30 and nine years a citizen.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the terms and the ages. House: 2-year terms, age 25; Senate: 6-year terms, age 30.

topics.title: Apportionment and Redistricting
topics.short: After each census the 435 House seats are divided among the states by population (every state gets at least one); states then draw districts, which must have nearly equal populations (Wesberry v. Sanders, 1964), after Baker v. Carr (1962) let courts hear such claims; drawing them for party or group advantage is called gerrymandering.
topics.trouble: Students think the number of House seats grows with each census. It has been fixed at 435 since 1913 (by law since 1929); states gain or lose seats as populations shift.

topics.title: The Powers of Congress
topics.short: Congress's enumerated powers include taxing, spending, borrowing, regulating commerce, coining money, declaring war and raising armies; each house has its own powers: the House starts revenue bills and impeaches, the Senate tries impeachments, confirms appointments and approves treaties.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the houses' special powers. The House impeaches (accuses); the Senate holds the trial. The Senate, not the House, confirms appointments and approves treaties.

topics.title: Leaders of Congress
topics.short: The Speaker of the House, chosen by the House, leads it; majority and minority leaders and whips organize each party; the Vice President is President of the Senate and votes only to break ties, with the President pro tempore presiding in his or her absence.
topics.trouble: Students think the Vice President runs the Senate day to day. The VP rarely presides; the Senate majority leader sets the agenda.

topics.title: Committees
topics.short: Most work happens in committees: standing (permanent, by subject), select or special (temporary), joint (both houses) and conference (to settle differences between House and Senate versions of a bill); committees hold hearings and mark up bills.
topics.trouble: Students think every bill gets a vote on the floor. Most bills die in committee without a vote.

topics.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
topics.short: A bill is introduced, sent to committee, debated and passed by one chamber, then the other; differences are resolved; the President signs it, vetoes it (Congress may override by two-thirds of each house) or lets it become law without a signature after ten days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is in session.
topics.trouble: Students think an unsigned bill always becomes law after ten days. If Congress adjourns during those ten days, the bill dies: a pocket veto.

topics.title: House Rules and the Senate Filibuster
topics.short: The House Rules Committee sets limits on debate and amendments; in the Senate debate is unlimited unless 60 senators vote for cloture, so a minority can block many bills by filibuster; budget reconciliation and nominations have special rules.
topics.trouble: Students think the filibuster is in the Constitution. It comes from Senate rules, which the Senate can change; supporters say it protects minority views, and critics say it blocks majorities.

topics.title: The Budget and Oversight
topics.short: Congress controls spending: discretionary spending is set each year by appropriations, while mandatory spending (Social Security, Medicare, interest) runs under existing laws; Congress oversees agencies through hearings, investigations and funding; "pork barrel" and logrolling describe trading support for projects.
topics.trouble: Students think most federal spending is decided fresh each year. Mandatory spending and interest make up most of the budget.

topics.title: How Members Represent
topics.short: Members may act as delegates (vote as constituents want), trustees (use their own judgment) or politicos (mix the two); divided government, partisanship and the pull of reelection shape their choices.
topics.trouble: Students think one role is the correct one. Each has a defense: delegates follow the people's wishes; trustees bring judgment and information. Most members blend them.

topics.title: Qualifications, Terms and Succession
topics.short: A President must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 and a resident for 14 years; the Twenty-second Amendment limits a President to two elected terms; the Vice President comes first in the line of succession, then the Speaker and the President pro tempore; the Twenty-fifth Amendment covers disability.
topics.trouble: Students think the Secretary of State is next after the Vice President. By the Presidential Succession Act of 1947, the Speaker of the House is next, then the President pro tempore, then the Cabinet starting with the Secretary of State.

topics.title: The President's Formal Powers
topics.short: The Constitution makes the President commander in chief and gives the powers to veto, to pardon, to make treaties and appoint officers with the Senate's consent, to receive ambassadors and to give Congress information on the State of the Union.
topics.trouble: Students think a presidential pardon can cover state crimes. The pardon power covers only federal offenses.

topics.title: Informal Powers and Tools
topics.short: Presidents also use powers not listed in the Constitution: executive orders, executive agreements with other countries, signing statements, the "bully pulpit" and party leadership.
topics.trouble: Students think an executive order can do anything a law can. It directs the executive branch under authority from the Constitution or a statute; courts can strike it down and a later President can revoke it.

topics.title: The Federal Bureaucracy
topics.short: The executive branch includes 15 Cabinet departments, independent agencies (such as NASA), independent regulatory commissions (such as the Federal Reserve Board, the SEC) and government corporations (such as the U.S. Postal Service); most employees are hired through a merit civil service.
topics.trouble: Students think the Cabinet is in the Constitution. The Constitution mentions "executive Departments" but no Cabinet; Washington began the practice, and Congress creates the departments by law.

topics.title: Holding the Bureaucracy Accountable
topics.short: Agencies write rules under authority Congress delegates; Congress checks them with hearings, budgets and new laws; the President appoints and directs leaders; courts review whether rules follow the law; iron triangles link agencies, committees and interest groups.
topics.trouble: Students think agencies make law on their own. Agency rules must rest on authority Congress has delegated and follow procedures; courts review them.

topics.title: Impeachment
topics.short: The House may impeach (formally accuse) by majority vote for "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors"; the Senate tries the case, and conviction takes two-thirds; Presidents Andrew Johnson (1868), Bill Clinton (1998) and Donald Trump (2019) were impeached and acquitted; Richard Nixon resigned (1974) before a House vote.
topics.trouble: Students think "impeached" means "removed." Impeachment is the charge; removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate, and no President has been removed.

topics.title: War Powers
topics.short: Congress declares war and funds the military; the President commands it; Congress has declared war only eleven times in five wars, and the War Powers Resolution (1973) requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours and to end action within 60 days (plus 30) without its approval.
topics.trouble: Students think every war was declared by Congress. Korea, Vietnam, the Gulf War and others were fought under resolutions, treaties or the President's authority without a declaration.

topics.title: The Federal Court System
topics.short: There are 94 district courts (trials), 13 courts of appeals (12 regional circuits plus the Federal Circuit) and the Supreme Court; federal courts hear cases about federal law and the Constitution, cases between states, and certain cases between citizens of different states.
topics.trouble: Students think the Supreme Court hears most appeals. It takes only about 60 cases a year from thousands of requests; for most cases the court of appeals has the final word.

topics.title: How the Supreme Court Decides
topics.short: Parties ask the Court to hear a case by a petition for certiorari; it takes a case when four justices agree (the rule of four); after briefs and oral argument the justices vote, and opinions are written for the majority, with concurring and dissenting opinions.
topics.trouble: Students think a dissent has no effect. A dissent is not law, but later Courts sometimes adopt its reasoning; Harlan's dissent in Plessy is a famous example.

topics.title: Judicial Review and Marbury v. Madison
topics.short: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court held that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional, establishing that federal courts may refuse to enforce laws that conflict with the Constitution.
topics.trouble: Students think Marbury won his job. The Court said he had a right to his commission but that it lacked power to order its delivery, because the law giving it that power was unconstitutional.

topics.title: Choosing Federal Judges
topics.short: The President nominates federal judges and the Senate confirms them by majority vote; they serve "during good Behaviour" (for life, unless impeached and removed), which is meant to make them independent of politics.
topics.trouble: Students think justices are elected or serve fixed terms. Federal judges are appointed and serve for life; many state judges, by contrast, are elected.

topics.title: Ways of Reading the Constitution
topics.short: Judges differ in method: originalists read the text as understood when it was adopted; living constitutionalists read its principles in light of changing conditions; judicial restraint favors deferring to elected branches and precedent, while "activism" is a label critics use for decisions they think go too far.
topics.trouble: Students equate originalism with "conservative" and living constitutionalism with "liberal" outcomes in every case. The methods are about how to read the text; judges of each school sometimes reach results that surprise people.

topics.title: Checks on the Courts
topics.short: The other branches check the courts by appointing and confirming judges, passing new laws after a statutory ruling, proposing amendments, setting the courts' size and some of their jurisdiction, and by how they carry out rulings; the courts have no army or budget of their own.
topics.trouble: Students think a Supreme Court ruling on a statute can only be undone by a constitutional amendment. If the ruling interprets a statute, Congress can simply amend the statute.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights, One by One
topics.short: Match each of the first ten amendments to what it protects: the First (religion, speech, press, assembly, petition) to the Tenth (powers reserved to the states or the people).
topics.trouble: Students mix up the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth. Fourth: searches and seizures; Fifth: self-incrimination, double jeopardy, due process, takings; Sixth: speedy public jury trial and a lawyer.

topics.title: Incorporation: Rights Against the States
topics.short: At first the Bill of Rights limited only the national government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833); through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause the Court has applied most of its protections to the states one by one, from Gitlow v. New York (1925) to McDonald v. Chicago (2010).
topics.trouble: Students think the whole Bill of Rights applied to the states from 1791. It was incorporated piece by piece in the twentieth century, and a few provisions (such as the grand jury requirement) still are not.

topics.title: Freedom of Religion
topics.short: The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing religion: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down a state-written prayer in public schools; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) let Amish families end formal schooling after eighth grade.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the two clauses. Establishment limits government sponsorship of religion; Free Exercise protects people's practice of religion. A case can involve both.

topics.title: Freedom of Speech
topics.short: Speech is broadly protected but not unlimited: Schenck v. United States (1919) used a "clear and present danger" test; Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students' armbands; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) protects advocacy unless it is aimed at and likely to produce imminent lawless action.
topics.trouble: Students think the First Amendment stops private companies or employers from limiting speech. It limits government; private parties are generally not bound by it.

topics.title: Freedom of the Press
topics.short: In New York Times v. United States (1971) the Court refused to stop newspapers from publishing the Pentagon Papers, applying a heavy presumption against prior restraint; New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) requires public officials suing for libel to prove "actual malice."
topics.trouble: Students think freedom of the press means the press cannot be sued. Publishers can be held liable for libel after publication; the strong protection is against censorship beforehand.

topics.title: The Right to Keep and Bear Arms
topics.short: In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) the Court held the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense; McDonald v. Chicago (2010) applied it to the states; the Court has said the right has limits.
topics.trouble: Students state one reading of the amendment as settled before 2008. Before Heller, courts and scholars debated whether the right was individual or tied to militia service; Heller adopted the individual reading 5 to 4, and four justices dissented.

topics.title: Rights of the Accused
topics.short: The Fourth, Fifth, Sixth and Eighth Amendments protect people suspected or accused of crimes: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied the exclusionary rule to the states; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed a lawyer for poor defendants charged with felonies; Miranda v. Arizona (1966) required warnings before custodial questioning.
topics.trouble: Students think police must read Miranda warnings at every arrest. Warnings are required before custodial interrogation; without them, statements generally cannot be used in the prosecution's main case.

topics.title: Privacy and Unenumerated Rights
topics.short: The Ninth Amendment says listing some rights does not deny others; the Court has recognized rights not named in the text through the Due Process Clause, and it disagrees about how to identify them: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) and Roe v. Wade (1973) recognized such rights, Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) asked whether a right is deeply rooted in history and tradition, and the Court overruled Roe in 2022.
topics.trouble: Students think the word "privacy" appears in the Constitution. It does not; the debate is over whether and how courts should recognize rights the text does not list. Present both sides' reasoning.

topics.title: Equal Protection
topics.short: The Fourteenth Amendment forbids states to deny "the equal protection of the laws"; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed "separate but equal," and Brown v. Board of Education (1954) held that separate schools are "inherently unequal."
topics.trouble: Students think equal protection forbids every law that treats groups differently. Laws classify people all the time (by age, income); courts ask how strong the reason is, and race and a few other classifications get the strictest review.

topics.title: Civil Rights Laws
topics.short: Congress used its powers to ban discrimination: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (public places, employment), the Voting Rights Act of 1965, Title IX of the Education Amendments (1972, sex discrimination in schools receiving federal funds) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990).
topics.trouble: Students think civil rights laws come only from the Fourteenth Amendment. Congress also relied on the Commerce Clause and the spending power, which let it reach private businesses.

topics.title: Widening the Vote
topics.short: Amendments expanded voting: the Fifteenth (race, 1870), Seventeenth (direct election of senators, 1913), Nineteenth (sex, 1920), Twenty-third (D.C. electors, 1961), Twenty-fourth (no poll taxes in federal elections, 1964) and Twenty-sixth (age 18, 1971).
topics.trouble: Students think the Constitution gives everyone a right to vote in so many words. The amendments forbid denying the vote on certain grounds; states set most voting rules within those limits.

topics.title: Majority Rule and Minority Rights
topics.short: Democracy rests on majority rule and on protecting minority rights; courts, the Bill of Rights, federalism and supermajority rules protect minorities, and debates over affirmative action, voting districts and religious exemptions show how hard the balance can be.
topics.trouble: Students think majority rule means the majority may do anything. Constitutional rights limit what any majority can enact.

topics.title: Becoming a Citizen
topics.short: People born in the U.S. (and most born abroad to citizen parents) are citizens; others may naturalize, generally after five years as a permanent resident (three if married to a citizen), at age 18 or older, by passing English and civics tests and taking the Oath of Allegiance.
topics.trouble: Students think naturalized citizens have fewer rights. They have the same rights, except that only natural-born citizens may be President or Vice President.

topics.title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizens
topics.short: Citizens have the right to vote, run for most offices and serve on juries; responsibilities include obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on a jury when called and, for men 18 to 25, registering with the Selective Service; civic habits such as staying informed are encouraged but not required.
topics.trouble: Students mix up legal duties and civic habits. Jury service when summoned and paying taxes are required by law; voting is a right that is not required in the United States.

topics.title: Voting and Turnout
topics.short: Citizens 18 and older may vote where they are registered; turnout is higher in presidential years than midterms and rises with age, education and interest; rules on registration, voting by mail and identification vary by state.
topics.trouble: Students think turnout is the same in every election. Midterm turnout has usually been well below presidential-year turnout.

topics.title: How Political Views Form
topics.short: Family, school, faith, peers, media and events shape political views; Americans also hold broad shared values (liberty, equality, democracy, individualism, the rule of law) and differ in ideology: liberals, conservatives and libertarians, each describing itself in its own terms.
topics.trouble: Students describe one ideology through its opponents' eyes. Use each group's own statement of its views; for example, libertarians favor limited government on both economic and personal questions.

topics.title: Public Opinion and Polls
topics.short: Polls estimate public opinion from a random sample; a good sample is random and large enough, questions are worded neutrally, and every poll has a margin of error (about plus or minus 3 points for 1,000 people).
topics.trouble: Students think a candidate ahead by 2 points with a 3-point margin of error is clearly winning. When the gap is within the margin of error, the race is too close for that poll to call.

topics.title: Interest Groups and the Media
topics.short: Interest groups lobby officials, file lawsuits and support candidates through PACs; the media report, set agendas and frame issues; concerns include unequal access, bias claims from all sides and the spread of false information.
topics.trouble: Students think lobbying is illegal bribery. Lobbying is protected petitioning, regulated by disclosure laws; bribery is a crime.

topics.title: Political Parties
topics.short: Parties recruit candidates, organize voters and run the government; the U.S. has a two-party system, encouraged by single-member districts with winner-take-all rules; third parties raise issues but rarely win.
topics.trouble: Students think the Constitution creates the two parties. Parties are not in the Constitution; the election rules make two large parties likely.

topics.title: Primaries, Caucuses and Conventions
topics.short: Parties choose presidential nominees through state primaries and caucuses that award delegates; closed primaries admit only party members, open primaries any registered voter; delegates nominate at the national convention.
topics.trouble: Students confuse primary and general elections. A primary picks a party's candidate; the general election in November picks the officeholder.

topics.title: The Electoral College
topics.short: Each state has electors equal to its House seats plus two senators, and D.C. has three (538 in all); a candidate needs 270; 48 states give all their electors to the statewide winner, while Maine and Nebraska also award electors by district; if no one has a majority, the House chooses, one vote per state delegation.
topics.trouble: Students think the national popular vote winner always wins. Five times (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016) the winner of the Electoral College was not the popular vote leader (in 1824 the House chose).

topics.title: Money in Campaigns
topics.short: Federal law limits and discloses contributions to candidates (FECA, 1971; BCRA, 2002); Buckley v. Valeo (1976) treated spending as protected speech; Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held the government may not limit independent spending by corporations and unions, which led to super PACs.
topics.trouble: Students think Citizens United allows unlimited donations directly to candidates. Direct contributions to candidates are still limited; the ruling concerned independent spending.

topics.title: Congressional Elections
topics.short: Most House members who seek reelection win, thanks to name recognition, fundraising and district lines (the incumbency advantage); the President's party usually loses seats in midterm elections.
topics.trouble: Students think Congress turns over a lot each election. Reelection rates for House incumbents who run have usually been above 90 percent.

topics.title: State Government
topics.short: Every state has its own constitution, a governor, a legislature (all bicameral except Nebraska's) and courts; states run elections, schools, most criminal law, licenses and roads.
topics.trouble: Students think most laws people meet day to day are federal. Traffic, family, property, most crimes and schools are mostly state and local law.

topics.title: Local Government
topics.short: Counties, cities and towns, school districts and special districts (water, fire, transit) provide many services; cities may use a mayor-council or a council-manager form; local governments get their powers from their state.
topics.trouble: Students think cities are independent like states. Local governments are created by and get their powers from the state.

topics.title: Initiative, Referendum and Recall
topics.short: Many states let voters propose laws or amendments by petition (the initiative), approve or reject laws (the referendum) and remove officials before their terms end (the recall); there is no national initiative or referendum.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the initiative and the referendum. The initiative starts with the voters' petition; a referendum sends a measure, often from the legislature, to the voters.

topics.title: Tribal Nations
topics.short: There are 575 federally recognized tribes (as of 2026); they are sovereign nations with their own governments and courts, in a government-to-government relationship with the United States set by the Constitution, treaties and federal law.
topics.trouble: Students think tribal nations are part of state governments. Tribes are sovereign governments; state law generally has limited reach on tribal lands.

topics.title: Citizenship Test: Government
topics.short: Practice questions like those on the naturalization civics test about principles of American democracy, the system of government, and rights and responsibilities.
topics.trouble: Learners memorize answers without the idea behind them, and a reworded question trips them up. Practice the reason behind each answer.

topics.title: Citizenship Test: History and Symbols
topics.short: Practice questions like those on the naturalization civics test about colonial times and independence, the 1800s, recent American history, geography, symbols and holidays.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up dates and documents (1776 and 1787, the Declaration and the Constitution). Anchor each answer on a timeline.
